caption_hook: Alabama holds a chalk sea floor, coal swamps, iron ore, cave country and famous white marble.

layers.name: DEMOPOLIS CHALK
layers.hook: A pale sea floor in the Black Belt
layers.what: A warm sea once covered central Alabama, and the shells of tiny plankton settled into soft white chalk. Mosasaurs, giant sea turtles and sharks left their bones in it.
layers.bonus: Its dark, rich soil is a big reason the Black Belt region got its name.

layers.name: POTTSVILLE FORMATION
layers.what: Giant ferns and club-mosses grew in swamps on a low, flat coast. Buried and squeezed for ages, their remains turned into the coal seams of the Warrior coalfield.
layers.bonus: Birmingham grew up because coal, iron ore and limestone all lay within a few miles.

layers.name: BANGOR LIMESTONE
layers.hook: A shallow sea full of future caves
layers.what: Warm, shallow seas piled up limy mud and shells that hardened into thick limestone. Rain slowly dissolved it into the sinkholes, springs and caves of northern Alabama.
layers.bonus: Cathedral Caverns near Grant has a giant stalagmite called Goliath, about 45 feet tall.

layers.name: RED MOUNTAIN FORMATION
layers.hook: Iron-rich rock that built a city
layers.what: Sand and mud on an ancient sea floor, rich in iron minerals, formed a long red ridge. Miners dug out the ore, and Birmingham's furnaces turned it into iron and steel.
layers.bonus: Vulcan, the world's largest cast-iron statue, stands on this ridge in Birmingham.

layers.name: SYLACAUGA MARBLE
layers.hook: The state rock, whiter than snow
layers.what: Ancient sea-floor limestone was baked and squeezed deep underground as mountains rose, recrystallizing into pure white marble. It is prized worldwide, and marble is Alabama's state rock.
layers.bonus: In 1954 a meteorite crashed through a roof in Sylacauga and bruised a woman napping on her couch.
